summary: Bicquette Island light, a 22.5 m stone tower in the St. Lawrence off Le Bic: Trinity House era, an 1853 grounding, keepers to 1987, now automatic and closed to visitors.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Quebec record: established and tower built 1843. LighthouseFriends, Radio-Canada and Les amis des phares: 1844. The 2006 UQAR article: 1841. Likely the tower was built in 1843 and first lit in 1844, but the sources do not say so outright.
Quebec record and federal statement name Montreal engineer Charles Atherton; LighthouseFriends names Joseph Archer as directing construction. Both may have a part; the sources do not reconcile them.
LighthouseFriends dates the wooden cladding to 1866; the federal statement says around 1900; the Quebec record says probably about 1902.
LighthouseFriends: third-order Fresnel lens, 1909, white flash every three seconds. Quebec record: first-order catoptric rotating light in the lantern. Not reconciled.
LighthouseFriends: 1883 and 1962. Quebec record: 1955 and 1961 replacing the 19th-century house. Not reconciled.
LighthouseFriends lists Hammond to 1857 but its text has him drowned in March 1859. The 1859 date stands in the text; the list end is reported as printed.

notes_for_editor: Sources conflict on the build year (1841/1843/1844), the designer (Atherton or Archer), the cladding date (1866 vs c.1900/1902), the lens (third-order Fresnel vs first-order catoptric), the dwellings (1883/1962 vs 1955/1961) and the access rules. The record's characteristic is disputed: LighthouseFriends describes a white flash every six seconds and/or a red flash every two seconds by direction of approach, OSM and Wikidata give Fl W 3s and Fl R 6s; no characteristic is put in facts. The ARLHS record (CAN-237) carries a 'structure removed' flag and was not used for any fact; it needs a human look. The 1859 drowning, the Fortier episode, the 1853 Berbice grounding and the 1875 fire rest on LighthouseFriends alone; no newspaper or Department report consulted confirms them. The Chronicling America search for 'Bicquette' found nothing relevant. The WWII German landing is recollection in a 2006 article and a 2016 headline; unconfirmed. The 1919 entry, printed as 'Biquette island' (OCR), names no vessel. The Sahara's own preliminary finding (scan pp. 49-50, printed pp. 36-37, checked on the page image) blames the captain for leaving Father Point too hastily. The 1902 report's other two findings, 'the master unwisely steering from a safe position off Bicquette' (Rustington, scan p. 46) and 'an error of judgment on the part of the pilot' (Manchester Importer, scan p. 48), belong to other ships and are not used for the Sahara. Keeper names from the Marine reports were not matched by column position for this station (the 1905 and 1915 keeper tables are column-blocked), so the roster follows LighthouseFriends; E. Heppel and E. Thibault are not linked to Elzear Heppel or Ernest Thibault. Maurice Thibault's connection ended in 1987; he is named only in his public role, with details the 2006 article prints. Radio-Canada's 2016 article carries a notice that it may be out of date. The Quebec record lists a fog-alarm shelter dated 1889; LighthouseFriends and the 1908-09 report date the wooden fog-alarm building to 1908. Not reconciled; the story follows the report. The 1841 date comes from the 2006 article only.
